title: RSIHub: A Composable Framework for Agent-Evolution Methods
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence

Title:RSIHub: A Composable Framework for Agent-Evolution Methods
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Agent-evolution methods use execution feedback to improve prompts, skills, tools, and orchestration, but their implementations often rebuild the same experimental machinery. We present RSIHub, an open-source framework for building, comparing, and extending these methods on shared infrastructure. Recipes compose reusable operators and declare mutable resources; RSIHub supplies execution, evaluation, recovery, and lineage. Researchers can focus on evolution policy while evaluation stays outside the mutable surface and results remain tied to candidates and evaluation conditions. We instantiate AHE, Hyperagents, A-Evolve, and GEPA without modifying the framework core, keeping method-specific logic in recipes and operators. We evaluate them with MiniSWE and Codex on Terminal Bench 2 and $\tau^3$ Banking under fixed model and evaluator configurations. The largest observed overall pass@1 gain is 13.5 percentage points, while method rankings vary across settings and optimization gains do not always transfer to held-out tasks. RSIHub provides a common protocol for comparing evolution policies, inspectable candidate histories, and reusable components for developing new methods.

report.summary: RSIHub is an open-source composable framework for building, comparing, and extending agent-evolution methods on shared execution, evaluation, and lineage infrastructure.
report.background: Agent-evolution methods—often grouped under self-improving or recursive self-improvement research—use execution feedback to rewrite prompts, skills, tool use, and orchestration policies. As interest has grown, labs and startups have released many one-off implementations, each with its own harness, logging, evaluator, and recovery logic. That makes comparisons fragile: gains may come from different model settings, evaluator quirks, or benchmark overfitting rather than the evolution policy itself. The field lacks a common protocol for isolating what actually improves an agent and for reproducing results. RSIHub responds to this infrastructure gap by treating evolution methods as recipes over reusable operators and mutable resources, while keeping evaluation outside the mutation surface. It also reflects a broader industry shift from hand-built agents toward measurable, iterative agent improvement loops, where lineage and held-out testing matter as much as headline benchmark scores.
key_points: RSIHub treats agent-evolution methods as recipes that compose reusable operators and declare mutable resources. The framework core supplies execution, evaluation, recovery, and lineage, so method-specific logic stays in recipes and operators rather than being rebuilt in each project. This lowers infrastructure duplication and makes components easier to reuse across experiments.

Evaluation is kept outside the mutable surface, and results remain tied to specific candidates and evaluation conditions. RSIHub also provides inspectable candidate histories. This design helps prevent evaluator tampering or benchmark overfitting and supports reproducibility, since researchers can trace which candidate produced which result under which conditions.

The authors instantiate four evolution methods—AHE, Hyperagents, A-Evolve, and GEPA—without modifying the framework core. This demonstrates that RSIHub can host distinct evolution policies under a common protocol. It also gives researchers a shared basis for comparing methods rather than relying on incompatible, one-off implementations.

Using MiniSWE and Codex on Terminal Bench 2 and tau^3 Banking under fixed model and evaluator configurations, RSIHub records a largest overall pass@1 gain of 13.5 percentage points. The result shows meaningful improvement potential, but it is tied to specific settings and evaluation conditions rather than being a universal claim.

Method rankings vary across settings, and optimization gains do not always transfer to held-out tasks. That finding is a warning against single-benchmark claims: an evolution policy that wins in one environment may not generalize. Held-out evaluation and careful reporting are essential when assessing self-improving agents.
report.impact: For the AI industry, RSIHub could become a shared benchmark protocol for agent self-improvement, making claims comparable and exposing evaluator leakage or overfitting. Developers get reusable execution, recovery, and lineage infrastructure, so they can focus on evolution policy rather than rebuilding harnesses; open recipes also lower the barrier to reproducing methods like GEPA or AHE. Regular users may eventually see more reliable agents because improvements are tested against held-out tasks, but the paper's mixed rankings and transfer gaps caution that self-evolution is not a guaranteed upgrade. The bigger shift is methodological: agent progress will be judged by reproducible, inspectable improvement loops, not one-off demo gains.
report.tools: Follow RSIHub's open-source release and paper for recipes, operators, and lineage tooling. Compare with GEPA, AHE, Hyperagents, and A-Evolve as reference evolution methods. For evaluation, watch MiniSWE and Codex agents on Terminal Bench 2 and tau^3 Banking; these harnesses are useful for testing whether gains transfer to held-out tasks. Also track related agent-evaluation frameworks and reproducible benchmark suites.
